Coursebook: Writing for Digital Media

Lecture videos and study packages — the essential materials for the exam. Watch the short lectures first, then work through the study package for each section.

Designed by Hamid Guedra (Language Centre, LAB University of Applied Sciences)

Introduction

Welcome!

This coursebook contains the essential materials for the exam. Please check the exam dates on the course page.

The coursebook includes short videos that introduce key topics, along with study packages that provide links to additional resources, primarily readings. Watch the short lecture videos before exploring the materials provided in the study packages.

Be an active student. 

  • I encourage you to save the readings as PDF files and take notes as you read. Most web browsers allow you to do this by right-clicking on a webpage and selecting Print and then Save as PDF.
  • You might also consider printing out some of the readings. Reading in print can be more effective than reading on a screen (see Reading print improves comprehension).

Finally, although the coursebook should work well on smartphones and tablets, it is best experienced on a laptop or desktop computer.

-Your instructor Hamid

And keep some of these nuggets of writing wisdom in mind:

  • "If you don't have time to read, you don't have the time (or the tools) to write." –Stephen King
  • "A word after a word after a word is power." –Margaret Atwood
  • "To write something you have to risk making a fool of yourself."  –Anne Rice
  • "You don't start out writing good stuff. You start out writing crap and thinking it's good stuff, and then gradually you get better at it. That's why I say one of the most valuable traits is persistence." –Octavia E. Butler
  • "One day I will find the right words, and they will be simple." –Jack Kerouac
  • "Easy reading is damn hard writing." –Nathaniel Hawthorne
  • "I notice that you use plain, simple language, short words and brief sentences. That is the way to write English – it is the modern way and the best way. Stick to it; don’t let fluff and flowers and verbosity creep in." –Mark Twain
  • "If people cannot write well, they cannot think well, and if they cannot think well, others will do their thinking for them." –George Orwell
  • "A skill is something you know how to do. Skill in writing frees you to write what you want to write. It may also show you what you want to write. Craft enables art." –Ursula Le Guin

Read / watch the following (related to the Key Vocabulary and Algospeak lectures).

A plain-English glossary of basic internet and email vocabulary — terms such as browser, download, URL, spam, and attachment — each with a short definition.

Link: https://www.englishclub.com/vocabulary/internet.php

Algospeak (“algorithm” + “speak”) is the use of coded words, alternative spellings, and emoji to get around the automated systems that flag, hide, or demonetise certain words on social platforms — and increasingly in search engines and email too. Creators substitute sensitive terms to keep content visible: “unalive” for suicide or death, or “mascara” as a euphemism when discussing intimate-partner violence. The argument is that algospeak lets people discuss important topics that moderation algorithms would otherwise suppress.

Link: https://www.algospeak.net/what-is-algospeak

A running glossary on the same site that lists algospeak terms next to their real meanings.

Link: https://www.algospeak.net/dictionary

Oxford University Press named “rage bait” its 2025 Word of the Year after more than 30,000 public votes (it beat “aura farming” and “biohack”). OUP defines it as online content deliberately designed to provoke anger or outrage in order to drive traffic and engagement; its usage tripled over the year. The choice reflects growing awareness of online manipulation tactics, the attention economy, and digital wellbeing.

Link: https://corp.oup.com/news/the-oxford-word-of-the-year-2025-is-rage-bait/

A reading on whether the word “internet” should be written with a capital I.

Link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rDf6GbGeuUtMqIFLAbjXhi_Cfb7l_o5M/view?usp=sharing

Investopedia traces three phases of the web. Web 1.0 (early 1990s to early 2000s) was a static, read-only web of simple pages. Web 2.0 — the current phase — is the read-write web of user-generated content and social networking. Web 3.0 is the emerging decentralised, open, AI- and blockchain-based web (sometimes called “read-write-execute”), intended to give users more control and ownership of their data.

Link: https://www.investopedia.com/web-20-web-30-5208698

In this Our World in Data piece, Max Roser (2018) argues that although the internet has already reshaped the world, the largest changes still lie ahead, because billions of people are only now coming online. He uses global adoption data to show how recent — and ongoing — the shift really is.

Link: https://ourworldindata.org/internet-history-just-begun

The linguist David Crystal on how the internet is changing everyday language.

Open on YouTube: https://youtu.be/P2XVdDSJHqY

A reading on how internet use is changing the English language.

Link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1DiQHD575AuroALtWBQBUdU2r2Cn5wHEe/view?usp=sharing

Study Package B: Participatory Culture

  • Approximate time to carefully study these materials: 5–7 hrs.

Start here:

  • Study Package B Summary
  • Study Package B Podcast

Both are AI-generated (NotebookLM) and cover only some of the materials below. Check them against the sources.

Read / watch the following (related to the Writing/Text and Participatory Culture lectures).

Jakob Nielsen (2006). In most online communities, participation follows a 90–9–1 pattern: roughly 90% of users are lurkers who only read, 9% contribute occasionally, and 1% produce almost all the content and activity. The implication is that what you see online is shaped by a tiny, unrepresentative minority, while the silent majority is never heard from.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/participation-inequality/

Jakob Nielsen. The web only reaches its potential when ordinary users create content rather than just consume it, but most people find authoring difficult. Proposed aids include structured-creation tools, selection-based media (such as picking the best of many photos — a 2020 update notes Instagram proved the point), and teaching content creation in schools.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/content-creation-for-average-people/

Boundless Marketing (Lumen). Defines social media as Web 2.0–based applications that let users create and exchange user-generated content (citing Kaplan and Haenlein), and frames digital marketing as using internet-connected devices to engage consumers — through “pull” methods (consumers seek the content) and “push” methods. Read Defining Social Media; you can stop at Social Media Marketing Communications.

Link: https://courses.lumenlearning.com/boundless-marketing/chapter/introduction-to-social-media-and-digital-marketing/

Investopedia. Defines social media as interactive, user-generated-content platforms and sketches the history: early personal-website services such as Geocities in the mid-to-late 1990s, SixDegrees in 1997, Friendster in 2002, then MySpace and LinkedIn — alongside the scale of global use today.

Link: https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/social-media.asp

Jakob Nielsen. Argues the web is not really a “community” — a huge, impersonal city is a better metaphor. User-generated content is valuable when it is edited, but features like chat rooms are undermined by participation inequality.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/community-is-dead-long-live-mega-collaboration

Nicholas Carr’s essay arguing that heavy internet use may be reshaping how we read and think — encouraging rapid skimming across many sources rather than sustained, deep reading.

Link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1hM7M8IOPC5v1uw4TMmCkA1Jpoj6buJit/view?usp=sharing

A discussion of how web culture affects reading, attention, and thinking.

Open on YouTube: https://youtu.be/MA_kxQTutbA

A discussion of Andrew Keen’s “cult of the amateur” critique of user-generated content.

Open on YouTube: https://youtu.be/un5vTaUZvi4

Toledo Museum of Art, on reading and interpreting visual information.

Open on YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=O39niAzuapc

Study Package C: Writing for the Web

  • Approximate time to carefully study these materials: 11–13 hrs.

Start here:

  • Study Package C Summary
  • Study Package C Podcast

Both are AI-generated (NotebookLM) and cover only some of the materials below. Check them against the sources.

Read / watch the following (related to the 4 Essential Types of Writing Styles and Writing for the Web lectures).

Grammarly. Outlines the four main writing styles — expository (explains or informs with facts), descriptive (evokes images), persuasive (argues a position with evidence), and narrative (tells a story) — and where each is typically used.

Link: https://www.grammarly.com/blog/types-of-writing/

Nielsen Norman Group. Short text — headlines, page titles, subject lines — carries disproportionate weight because people scan and decide fast, often forming opinions or sharing based on the title alone. Front-load keywords, keep titles short, and drop leading “the/a” in page titles.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/microcontent-how-to-write-headlines-page-titles-and-subject-lines/

Nielsen Norman Group. Treat headings as scannable microcontent: front-load keywords (readers fixate on the first few words), be specific and benefit-focused, sound authentic, make sense out of context, and minimise hype and idioms.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/headings-pickup-lines/

Video (Nielsen Norman Group). Eye-tracking shows people often scan pages in the shape of an F; the video revisits what the pattern means today.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/videos/f-pattern-reading-digital-content/

Nielsen Norman Group. Eye-tracking confirms that people scan rather than read, with only a minority reading word-for-word; scanning patterns have stayed remarkably stable over time. Front-load key information and structure content for scanning.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-people-read-online/

Nielsen Norman Group. Identifies four text-scanning patterns (worst to best for the reader): F-pattern, spotted, layer-cake, and commitment. Support scanning by chunking content into sections and bulleted lists, using meaningful subheadings, and styling keywords.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/text-scanning-patterns-eyetracking/

Nielsen Norman Group. When headings and subheadings are descriptive and visually distinct, readers scan efficiently from heading to heading — a gaze pattern resembling the layers of a cake — and find what they need quickly.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/layer-cake-pattern-scanning/

Jakob Nielsen (2008). On an average visit, users read at most about 28% of the words on a page — 20% is more realistic. A strong argument for concise, scannable writing.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-little-do-users-read/

The Website Architect. Left-aligned text is generally the most readable; justified text creates uneven word spacing that hampers reading, and centred text is difficult for many readers (including those with dyslexia), so it is best reserved for very short passages.

Link: https://thewebsitearchitect.com/does-center-aligned-text-matter-for-accessibility/

Video (Nielsen Norman Group) on writing effective bulleted lists for the web.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/videos/tips-bulleted-lists-digital-content/

A reading on why generative-AI chatbots produce confident but false information, and what that means for using them in writing and research.

Link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1E-QpbBEiDAiWu6C9vZUR1Q7Y46fipIlV/view?usp=sharing

A guide to plain-English writing: short words and sentences, the active voice, and cutting jargon.

Link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PW4LVW28pNZ_Y_CAWqZETiHFAaTL_BNz/view?usp=sharing

Nielsen Norman Group. Long-winded, jargon-heavy language sounds pretentious and alienates readers; replace vague jargon and complicated words with plain, common terms.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/cringeworthy-words/

Video (Nielsen Norman Group). Jakob’s Law: users spend most of their time on other sites, so they prefer yours to work the same way as the ones they already know.

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/videos/jakobs-law-internet-ux/

Rutgers University (Naaman, Boase and Lai). About 80% of regular users are “meformers,” who post about their own lives, feelings, and activities, while about 20% are “informers,” who share information and news; informers have larger, more interactive networks and roughly twice the followers.

Link: https://www.rutgers.edu/news/study-reveals-two-types-twitter-users

Naaman, Boase and Lai (2010), the academic paper (CSCW conference) behind the meformer / informer finding. You can skip the Method and Analysis sections.

Link: http://infolab.stanford.edu/~mor/research/naamanCSCW10.pdf

Influencer Marketing Hub. Reviews character limits across platforms and argues shorter is usually better: even where limits are large (e.g. Facebook), short posts engage more, and LinkedIn truncates around 140 characters (≈100 ideal).

Link: https://influencermarketinghub.com/best-length-for-social-media-posts

Nielsen Norman Group. Any piece of digital copy can be placed on four scales: humour (funny ↔ serious), formality (formal ↔ casual), respectfulness (respectful ↔ irreverent), and enthusiasm (enthusiastic ↔ matter-of-fact).

Link: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/tone-of-voice-dimensions/

Aino Juurikkala (2021), LUT master’s thesis. Examines how using a conversational human voice (CHV) — a personal, informal, responsive style — rather than a traditional corporate voice on Instagram shapes young audiences’ perceptions of a brand. Best Practices for Digital Writing

Knowing how to post is easy. Digital literacy is knowing why: which platform, which strategy, and for which reader. This section starts with how readers think — and then turns that into five writing habits.

How readers think: System 1 and System 2

In Thinking, Fast and Slow, Daniel Kahneman distinguishes two modes of thinking. Online readers arrive in System 1 — and decide within about 10 seconds whether your page is worth their System 2 (Nielsen Norman Group). If they don't immediately see the value proposition — why this content matters to them — they leave.

System 1 — fast

  • Automatic, quick, effortless; always running
  • Driven by habit, emotion, and first impressions
  • Scans titles, images, and topic sentences in seconds
  • Decides: stay or bounce?

System 2 — slow

  • Deliberate, logical, effortful — and "lazy"
  • Engages only when System 1 signals relevance or difficulty
  • Evaluates evidence, weighs options, reads carefully
  • This is the reader you are writing for — but you must get past System 1 first

The five habits

Click each habit to open its strategies.

  • Put the main idea in the title. "10 Best Vacation Spots in Indiana" beats "Pack Your Bags" — the value proposition must be visible at a glance.
  • Use descriptive headings and subheadings so scanners can follow the main ideas.
  • Front-load the most important information.
  • Keep language and sentence structure simple — conversational, no alienating jargon.
  • Use precise language. Vague writing ("recent studies", "severely injured") invites the question "can you be more specific?"
  • Use hyperlinks to clarify, build credibility, and point readers to sources.
  • Repeat keywords so readers can track the main idea from title to body.

Most readers don't read web pages word for word — they scan, taking in roughly 20% of the text on a page (Nielsen Norman Group).

  • Condense: cut redundancies and filler words.
  • Chunk content: digital paragraphs run about 2–5 sentences; break long texts into headed sections.
  • Use hyperlinks instead of elaborating on everything in the text.
  • Use bullets so key points survive scanning.
  • Prefer the active voice: "Jenny made a cake" rather than "A cake was made by Jenny."
  • Eliminate "be" verbs where possible: "We will eat at 5 p.m." rather than "We will be eating at 5 p.m."

Unprofessional writing reads as self-centred, unfocused, or lazy. Professional writing builds credibility:

  • Avoid slang that excludes part of your audience.
  • Never use offensive language — a hard rule, in any genre.
  • Stick to your purpose: one clear main idea, no tangents.
  • Be respectful: invite calm, reasoned engagement with differing views.
  • Proofread: error-filled writing is hard to read and signals low effort.

Monitoring means tracking and responding to reactions on your channels — your replies become part of a public thread that shapes how others see you.

  • Respond thoughtfully to at least some positive feedback.
  • Answer relevant questions completely and specifically.
  • Engage respectfully with negative comments — other readers are watching.
  • Don't delete every negative comment; do delete offensive or threatening ones.
  • Monitor brand mentions elsewhere: reviews, tags, hashtags, @ mentions.

Most digital messages end with a CTA (call to action) — an explicit statement of what the reader should do next, with everything they need to do it: click a link, subscribe, reply by a deadline, schedule a meeting. Clear, direct instructions get more responses than hints.

Try it: tighten the sentence

Each example below breaks a concision rule. Decide how you would rewrite it, then reveal one possible revision.

"It was decided by the committee that the deadline will be being extended by a period of one week's time."
One revision: "The committee extended the deadline by one week." (Active voice, no "be" verbs, filler removed.)
"There are many people who are of the opinion that remote work is something that can be considered to be quite beneficial."
One revision: "Many people consider remote work beneficial." (Cut "there are" and nested filler phrases.)
"A recent study showed that wearing a seat belt is important and can severely reduce injuries in some situations."
One revision: Name the study, the year, and the figure: "A 2023 study by [organisation] found seat belts reduced serious injuries by [X]%." Precision, not vagueness — and hyperlink the study.

Writing the Genres of the Web

A genre is a category of writing with recognisable features. A genre convention is one of those defining features — and it exists for a social reason: audiences expect certain patterns, and following them improves readability and your credibility. Genre has been called a "typified rhetorical action" (Oregon State University): features repeat because audiences want certain experiences.

Why conventions matter

The grocery list test

Imagine a grocery "list" written as a full-sentence paragraph, every item explained and run together. Same information — but you'd miss half the items. The convention (one short item per line) is the function.

The résumé test

Black legible type, name and contact details on top, clear headings, one page. These conventions let an employer scan and decide quickly — and they signal that you know the genre. Emojis on a résumé would cost you the job before the content was read.

Four web genres and their conventions

More formal than texting; two professional types: (1) work emails to colleagues, clients, or vendors — friendly but to the point, chunked, with a CTA; (2) marketing-campaign emails, with conventions of their own:

  • Clear subject line — specific and under ~60 characters so it isn't cut off.
  • Preview text — a subtitle-style hook, typically ≤45 characters.
  • Keep it short — a couple of paragraphs.
  • Clear CTA — usually a link back to the website.
  • Contact information in a professional signature.

The website is the "front door" — "the center of your digital ecosystem" (Dieno). Five core functions: attract visitors (inbound marketing, meta descriptions, meta tags), provide useful content (no keyword stuffing), strengthen the brand, prompt action (CTAs), and generate leads (ethically — no deceptive collection).

Conventions:

  • Streamline content — sometimes less is more.
  • Most important information first (the inverted pyramid).
  • Intentional organisation: group like content, logical navigation, clear labels; plan with a site map.
  • Readability: headings, bullets, short paragraphs, sans serif fonts.
  • Be specific — readers want dimensions, prices, dates, not flowery vagueness.
  • Hyperlinks (internal and external) that match reader expectations.
  • Purposeful visuals; appealing aesthetics; clear CTAs; content kept up to date.

Blogs keep a website fresh, build expertise, and drive traffic. Every successful blog has a niche — focused enough to build a brand, broad enough to sustain 10–15+ article ideas (student success, not just study skills; DIY, not just window replacement).

  • Stay focused on the niche and the advertised topic.
  • Chunk content into headed subsections.
  • Be concise: 2–4-sentence paragraphs, bullets, simple structures.
  • Engaging, specific titles ("Reduce Your Debt in Three Easy Steps").
  • Hyperlink to credible, current sources; some internal links, sparingly.
  • Friendly, conversational tone — yet professional.
  • Visuals to break up text; careful proofreading.
  • Update often (date your posts); end with a CTA.

Professionally, social media is targeted, fast, and cheap. Organisations choose platforms where their audience actually is, plan a social media calendar, and fill it from content buckets (e.g. employee profiles, testimonials, product highlights). Content must match the platform's theme and format.

  • Be concise — get the main idea into a sentence or two before the "read more" fold.
  • Use 2–3 researched hashtags, not 7–10.
  • Title professional posts to carry the value proposition.
  • Use appealing images or short videos.
  • Give full URLs (or a button) — many platforms don't do inline hyperlinks.
  • Include a CTA; stay engaged in the comment thread.

Try it: which genre is this convention from?

Each convention below is most characteristic of one genre. Pick one.

"Preview text of 45 characters or fewer, shown after the subject line."
"Pick a niche broad enough to support 10–15 future article ideas."
"Organise pages with a site map: group like content, logical navigation, clear labels."
"Use two or three researched hashtags and give the full URL rather than an inline hyperlink."

Meeting a new genre?

You will. The method: gather several examples of the genre and reverse-engineer the conventions — typical content, tone of voice, design elements, organisational structure. Once you understand the concept of genre conventions, you can learn any new genre with confidence.

Basic Design Principles

The user experience (UX) covers "all aspects of the end user's interaction" with an organisation (Nielsen Norman Group) — and online, it begins with a snap System 1 judgement based on visual cues. Design is rhetoric: every layout choice answers What should my audience know? What should they do?

Six foundational principles

  • Limit information on the page — too much overwhelms.
  • Emphasise the most important items — higher, bigger, set apart.
  • Stick with what readers know — familiar patterns (navigation at the top) free attention for content.
  • Balance positive elements and white space so no area overwhelms the rest; designers plan with grids and wireframes.

Directs attention through placement, size, and contrast: titles big and on top; CTA buttons set apart by colour and negative space. Familiar scanning patterns — the F-pattern and Z-pattern — match how readers' eyes naturally move.

  • Proximity: close items read as related (caption under photo).
  • Common region: a shared box or background colour groups items (navigation bar).
  • Similarity: matching borders, colours, fonts, and sizes signal equal weight and relatedness.

Consistent page structure, colour scheme, fonts, and element treatments (all CTA buttons look alike) make a design unified, intuitive, and on-brand. Imagine the alternative: random fonts and colours everywhere — unreadable and untrustworthy.

Multiple modes — images, colour, text, video — engage and clarify. Variety and consistency coexist: use the same two or three colours varied across the page. Don't go overboard; when everything is emphasised, nothing is.

Only sharp, well-lit, well-framed photos; only videos with clean audio, steady camera work, and good pacing. Editing tools help, but start from quality — poor media undermines everything else on the page.

Gestalt design principles — click to explore

Gestalt psychology studies how people perceive a layout as a whole, not as isolated parts. Seven classic principles:

Similarity

Items with shared features group together — or one different item stands out from the group.

Good figure / simplicity

Viewers reduce complex designs to their simplest form (the Olympic logo reads as five circles).

Proximity

Items near each other read as related; distance makes items stand apart.

Continuity

The mind connects items along a line or curve — lining items up sequences how readers process them.

Closure

Viewers fill in gaps: a dotted outline still reads as a circle, not scattered dots.

Figure / ground

We separate focal point from background — put what matters in the foreground, contrasted.

Common fate

Items moving or pointing the same way (e.g. italics sharing an angle) group together.

Colour theory and typography

Colour theory

  • Hue, shade, saturation: brighter, more saturated colours carry more visual weight.
  • Emotion: warm colours (red, orange, yellow) vs cool (blue, purple, green); red ↔ love/anger/warmth, yellow ↔ happiness — choose to match tone (laser tag ≠ funeral home).
  • Combination: complementary vs analogous palettes; emphasis works only against de-emphasis. Keep a consistent palette.

Typography

  • Size: roughly 11 pt or larger for digital body text; bigger when read from a distance.
  • Font choice: sans serif for body text; expressive fonts only for short, large display text — and matched to tone (no Curlz on a wedding invitation).
  • Contrast: text must stand out from its background — light grey on white fails; over images, use negative space, shadows, or text boxes.

Special considerations for digital design

  • File sizes: web images need only ~72 dpi (vs 300 for print); use .jpg/.png; compress or embed videos via YouTube to keep load times short.
  • Cascading style sheets: style choices defined once apply consistently across pages — most platforms build this in.
  • Hyperlinks and buttons: follow the universal signals (blue underlined links; visited-link colour change; recognisable buttons for CTAs).
  • Mobile responsiveness: layouts must reformat for each device, not just shrink.
  • Testing: digital design is easy to change — use metrics (time on page, CTA clicks) to iterate.

Practice Quiz

Ten questions across all three chapters. Choose an answer to see immediate feedback. Your score appears at the bottom.
1. According to Kahneman, System 1 thinking is best described as…
System 1 operates "automatically and quickly with little or no effort". System 2 is the slow, effortful, deliberate mode — and it's lazy.
2. Research by the Nielsen Norman Group suggests you must communicate your value proposition within roughly…
The first ten seconds of a page visit are critical: if readers don't immediately see why the content is relevant, they bounce before System 2 ever engages.
3. Which title best follows the "Be Clear" guidelines for a blog post?
The title should carry the main idea and the value proposition. Cryptic or overly creative titles fail the 10-second test, even with interested readers.
4. Which sentence is the most concise revision of "The report was being written by the team over the course of last week"?
Active voice, no "be" verbs, no filler: subject (team) → verb (wrote) → object (report).
5. A genre convention is best defined as…
Conventions repeat "because audiences expect certain things to happen" — genre is a "typified rhetorical action" (Oregon State University). Following conventions builds credibility and readability.
6. Which of the following is NOT one of the five core website functions described in the chapter?
The five functions are attract visitors, provide useful content, strengthen the brand, prompt action, and generate leads. Other channels (blogs, social media, email) feed the website — they aren't replaced by it.
7. A hardware store starts a blog about DIY projects and home repairs. This illustrates…
A niche should relate to the brand and be broad enough to sustain many article ideas — DIY does both for a hardware store, drawing readers who then buy tools.
8. The navigation bar groups its links in a shared white strip at the top of the page. Which Gestalt principle is doing the work?
Common region: items set apart in a shared enclosed area or background colour are perceived as a group.
9. For large blocks of body text on screen, the chapter recommends…
Readability first: sans serif body text, sufficient size, and clear contrast with the background. Expressive fonts belong in short, large display text matched to the message's tone.
10. A mobile-responsive website is one that…
Responsive design reformats — key items resize and stack vertically — rather than merely shrinking the desktop layout.
Score: 0 / 10 answered: 0
